meta.title: Lao A2 Elementary
meta.subtitle: 750 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Lao → English (see the Lao, recall the meaning) and English → Lao (see an English meaning, recall the Lao). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 750 words for an elementary learner, aligned to A2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand sentences and frequently used expressions related to areas of most immediate relevance' — a learner here is able to manage simple, routine exchanges of information on familiar matters — personal and family information, shopping, the local area, work — and to describe in simple terms their background, their surroundings and what they immediately need. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Lao, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 389 of the 750 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — relatives and the people around you, jobs, work and study, clothes, more food, cooking and eating out, the things of a home, the town and its buildings, travel and directions, the countryside, nature, weather and animals, the seasons, health and the body, feelings and character, free time, sport and festivals, money, tools, telling what happened and comparing, and the everyday verbs of moving, dressing and doing — and the other 361 are the commonest remaining words of Lao, counted in the articles of the Lao Wikipedia. The greetings and pronouns are dealt first and the rest in that frequency order. Every meaning comes from English Wiktionary, whose Lao is far smaller than its Thai, and a handful of everyday words it has no entry for — among them ວ່າ, ຍັງ, ເອົາ and ຢາກ — are left out rather than given a meaning written here. Every headword is printed in Lao script with a romanisation beneath it: the sounds as Wiktionary transcribes the Vientiane pronunciation, written in the style of the Paiboon system the Thai decks use (a doubled vowel is long; ɛ, ɔ, ʉ and ə are the vowels of English 'bed', 'law', a 'u' said with spread lips, and 'the'), and after each syllable its TONE drawn as a pitch line in Chao tone letters — ˧˥ rising, ˩˧ low rising, ˧ mid, ˥˨ high falling, ˧˩ low falling — because a Lao word said on the wrong tone is a different word. The Lao Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the script and the rules that decide a tone. 42 nouns show the classifier they are counted with, and there are no forms to learn: Lao words never change shape. Example sentences come with 61 of the 750 words, three apiece for 14 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword; Tatoeba holds only some 230 Lao sentences, so most come from Wiktionary. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, pronunciation, classifiers and some example sentences: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: word counts made from the Lao Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0); no Wikipedia text is in the deck. Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR, and Wiktionary.

ເມື່ອຫລຽວເຫັນຕອນທຳອິດ, ການຂຽນແບບນີ້ອາດຈະເບິ່ງຄືວ່າ ບໍ່ມີຫຍັງຫລວງຫລາຍ, ແຕ່ທັງໝົດນີ້ມັນໄດ້ຖືກຂຽນອອກມາໂດຍຜ່ານການໃຊ້ຄວາມຄິດທັງນັ້ນ. ໃນຂະນະທີ່ຜູ້ເຂົ້າຮ່ວມການທົດລອງວາດພາບເບິ່ງການຂຽນໂຕໜັງສື ຫຼື ສັນຍາລັກຢູ່ນັ້ນ, ເຄື່ອງເຊັນເຊີ ຫລືເຄື່ອງຈັບສັນຍານທີ່ຝັງຢູ່ໃນສະໝອງ ຂອງລາວຈະຈັບເອົາຮູບແບບຂອງກິດຈະກຳທາງໄຟຟ້າໄດ້, ເຊິ່ງຫຼັງຈາກນັ້ນ ລະບົບຄິດໄລ່ຂອງເຄື່ອງຄອມພິວເຕີກໍຕີຄວາມໝາຍກິດຈະກຳນັ້ນໆ ເພື່ອ ຕິດຕາມເບິ່ງບ່ອນທີ່ປາຍປາກກາຢູ່ໃນມະໂນພາບນັ້ນຂຽນໄປ.

U.S. Ambassador Dr. Peter M. Haymond handed over 93 containers of fortified rice, lentils, canned fish and fortified cooking oil to Deputy Minister of Education and Sports, Dr. Sisouk Vongvichith at the World Food Programme’s (WFP) warehouse in Vientiane today. The food will be used to prepare healthy school lunches for 63,000 school children around Lao PDR.
